“You only need to find one person in this entire world who doesn’t find you completely insufferable.”
That’s the wisdom Taylor Swift dispenses near the end of “Cleveland!,” from a newly expanded edition of “ The Life of a Showgirl ,” and if that exclamation point doesn’t tell you she’s found that person then I don’t know what would.
Released Thursday night, almost exactly a year after the original album came out, “ The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore ” tacks four bonus songs onto the blockbuster 2025 LP that set a record for the biggest opening week of all time even as it drew the harshest reviews of her career. It also follows Swift’s high-profile wedding in July — her husband, the NFL star Travis Kelce, grew up in Cleveland Heights — and comes just as Grammy voters are about to decide on nominations for February’s awards ceremony, where “The Life of a Showgirl” is eligible for Swift’s eighth album of the year nod. (In case you haven’t been keeping track, that would tie her with Frank Sinatra for the most in Recording Academy history.)
In a statement ahead of “The Encore’s” release, Swift said she’d taken a trip to Sweden to celebrate “Showgirl’s” success with Max Martin and Shellback, her two principal collaborators on the album. “Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in,” she wrote, “but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs.”
Here are the four “Encore” tracks, ranked from worst to best.
4. ‘Cleveland!’ The exclamation point really is hilarious. (No shots at Cleveland.) I kind of dig the airy jangle-pop production, which reminds me a bit of “Ruin the Friendship,” by far the best song on the original “Showgirl.” But writing about her and Kelce’s romance as a bulwark against all the hate she receives as a rich and powerful pop star feels pretty uninspired, at least as rendered here. “The taste of me is acquired, but it’s his favorite dish”? Alas, no.
3. ‘Patient Zero’ “Encore’s” lead single — with a splashy music video set to premiere during Sunday night’s MTV Video Music Awards — has Swift fielding a phone call from a woman who’s dating one of the singer’s exes and could use a little advice. (“I’ve gotta be honest — I’ve been expecting your call,” Swift tells her.) That’s a rich premise, and I like the way the unexpected fiddle lick scrapes against the glossy synths. Again, though, the lyrics lack the emotional sophistication with which she once would have told a story like this one. And the song’s central image — a guy with a “devil on his shoulder under his halo” — is downright awkward.
2. ‘Pink Clouding’ OK, now we’re getting somewhere. This shimmering electro-pop number takes its title, as I just learned, from a term used among people experiencing addiction to describe the temporary euphoria one might feel in the early stages of recovery. (Recall that Swift wrote “Lavender Haze” a few years ago after hearing the phrase on “Mad Men.”) Here she’s looking back with regret at a relationship that she can see now was clearly a rebound: “You met me at a cursed time / I told you I was fine / And you were so good / That’s why you haunt me like you should.”
1. ‘Babylon’ Look, I’m not crazy about “liberated libertine.” And “Love is ice upon the ladder that you need to climb”? It’s giving Airbnb wall art. But man, oh man, does Swift finally tap into something deep in “Encore’s” closer: a trembling acoustic-guitar ditty about someone who’s realized only too late what they let slip away. Listen for yourself to hear how she sings it — this is a beautifully tender vocal performance — but the verse about the all-but-abandoned young mom sneaking into the bathroom to call her mom is an absolute killer. Taylor Swift: good songwriter!

articles.content_orig:
New details about the recovery facility where Presley Gerber died are putting its founder’s past under scrutiny. Reza Nabavi , the psychologist who founded Resolutions Living in Santa Monica, California, had two drug-related arrests in 2002 and initially encountered problems obtaining professional registration because of his criminal history, according to records cited by Page Six and other outlets. California Board of Psychology records also document later disciplinary proceedings involving Nabavi.
The revelations have emerged days after Gerber, the 27-year-old son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died on September 20, 2026. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner recorded his place of death as a rehabilitation facility but has not yet established an official cause of death.
Santa Monica police are investigating the death as a suspected overdose . Authorities have said there is currently no indication of foul play, while toxicology testing is expected to play a key role in determining what happened.
Nabavi is a licensed clinical psychologist and founder of Resolutions Therapeutic Services. His professional biography says he specializes in substance-use disorders, mood and anxiety disorders, process addictions, and co-occurring conditions.
But recently resurfaced records have drawn attention to events from more than two decades ago. According to official documents reviewed by Page Six and subsequently reported by TMZ and Infobae , Oakland police arrested Nabavi in February 2002, when he was 25 years old. Officers reportedly discovered him asleep in a vehicle in an area authorities associated with frequent narcotics and prostitution activity.
A 15-year-old girl was reportedly inside the vehicle. According to accounts of the records, she told police she did not know Nabavi well and was under the influence of methamphetamine.
Police reportedly found methamphetamine, marijuana, a firearm, ammunition, and a hunting knife while searching the vehicle.
In May 2002, Nabavi pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor controlled-substance possession charge and received 36 months of probation, according to reports based on the records.
Later that month, he was arrested again following an incident in which he allegedly agreed to sell methamphetamine to an informant. Authorities reportedly recovered methamphetamine, marijuana, and a glass pipe during the subsequent search.
Nabavi again pleaded no contest to misdemeanor possession of a controlled substance and received another 36-month probation sentence, according to Infobae’s review of the records.
The decades-old cases later became relevant when Nabavi sought professional registration in psychology.
Nabavi reportedly applied to the California Board of Psychology for professional registration in 2004. His application was denied, according to reports citing board documents. The cited reasons included his criminal conviction, use of a controlled substance, and conduct considered relevant to professional psychology practice. Another application was denied in 2005.
He eventually obtained registration as a psychological assistant in January 2006. The following month, that registration was revoked, but the revocation was stayed while Nabavi was placed under conditions that reportedly included supervision, substance testing, and participation in a drug and alcohol recovery program.
Nabavi ultimately became registered as a psychologist in December 2006 after complying with the conditions imposed on him, according to the records cited in recent reporting.
California Board of Psychology meeting minutes confirm that Nabavi later petitioned for termination of his probation in May 2008. His current psychology license is reported as active through June 30, 2028.
The distinction between a rehabilitation center and a sober-living residence has become an important part of the Presley Gerber case. Although the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner classified Gerber’s place of death as a rehabilitation facility, California authorities have reportedly said Resolutions Living is not licensed as a residential substance-use disorder treatment facility.
The California Department of Health Care Services told TMZ that it has no record of Resolutions operating as a licensed substance-use disorder residential treatment facility in Santa Monica. Based on available information, the agency said the program appeared to operate as a sober-living environment or recovery residence.
Sober-living residences can operate without the same state license required for facilities providing residential substance-use treatment.
Resolutions Therapeutic Services separately advertises outpatient mental-health and addiction services. Its website identifies Nabavi as its founder and executive clinical director.
Gerber reportedly arrived at the Santa Monica facility on the evening of Saturday, September 19, only hours before his death.
The Los Angeles Times reported that Santa Monica police received calls concerning both a cardiac arrest and an overdose at Resolutions Living the following morning. Officers responded at approximately 9:35 a.m., and Gerber was pronounced dead shortly afterward.
Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death, including the possible source of drugs involved in the suspected overdose. However, the medical examiner has deferred the official cause and manner of death while toxicology testing is completed.
Although law enforcement is investigating an apparent or suspected overdose, an overdose has not yet been officially established as Gerber’s cause of death.
There is also currently no public finding that Nabavi or Resolutions Living caused Gerber’s death.
Before his death, Gerber had discussed his experiences with mental health and substance use .
In one of his final social media posts, he documented undergoing an ibogaine treatment as part of his efforts to address addiction. The model had also spoken publicly about depression and substance-use struggles and had launched a social media series focused on mental health.
Gerber was the only son of Crawford and Rande Gerber and the older brother of model and actress Kaia Gerber. He had established his own modeling career, working with major fashion brands including Calvin Klein and Dolce & Gabbana.
His family has asked for privacy following his death.

articles.title_orig: Five burning questions for the WNBA playoffs: Can the Lynx win first title since 2017? Will Liberty, Dream vanquish first-round demons?
articles.title_zh: Five burning questions for the WNBA playoffs: Can the Lynx win first title since 2017? Will Liberty, Dream vanquish first-round demons?
articles.content_orig:
The mad dash to seeding after the FIBA World Cup break proved that the next month will be tense, chaotic and full of good postseason basketball.
After the WNBA needed the entirety of its regular season to lock in postseason seeds — all of which were still available about 48 hours ahead of the season close — the playoffs will tip on Sunday with a full slate of games.
The tight nature of the standings and the close games throughout the year could spell a WNBA Finals series that bucks the trend of top-two seeds. The field is more wide-open than any in recent memory, combined with an offensive explosion and parity near the top. The format, which begins as a 1-1-1 best-of-three, lends itself to early upsets.
As the playoffs get underway, here are five big-picture questions to answer by the time the confetti falls.
The last two Lynx runs have ended in utter heartbreak and theatrics. Who can forget the iconic " this s*** was stolen from us " ending to the 2024 Finals against New York that went a full five games? The front office then ran the starting five back for 2025, but fell to Phoenix in the semifinals amid head coach Cheryl Reeve's theatrical technical, MVP runner-up Napheesa Collier 's injury and the ensuing scorched-earth exit interview blasting WNBA leadership .
For a second consecutive season, the Lynx lead the league in net rating (they were second in 2024). They added the best midseason addition in Collier, who returned in July from surgery on both of her ankles. And they have Olivia Miles, the presumptive Rookie of the Year, who is also a leading MVP candidate. Reeve and the rest of the front office switched up the roster, losing two major million-dollar frontcourt additions, but haven't missed a beat in the revamp around backcourt mates Courtney Williams and Kayla McBride .
Olivia Miles helped hold down the fort while Napheesa Collier rehabbed an injury. Now the duo aims to get Minnesota back to the mountaintop. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
"I want to see that F-you about us, and I mean that wholeheartedly," McBride, a 13-year veteran still chasing an elusive championship, told local reporters at practice this week. "I don't care about the [standings] outcomes. I'm more so concerned about our FU towards other teams and just going and taking and ripping people's hearts out and taking momentum back."
That attitude didn't land against the Fever on Tuesday. They have the pieces; can they channel that anger from two seasons of being the regular-season best, but not the champion, and tread the right side of luck? A championship would deliver the WNBA's all-time record to Minnesota. The Lynx won four titles every other year between 2011 and 2017. It's often joked that the Lynx only win in those odd years. Seattle won four, in '04, '10, '18 and '20. The defunct Houston Comets franchise won four straight from 1997 to 2000.
The World Cup break is in some ways regular, in others unprecedented. The WNBA takes international breaks for the Olympics from mid-July to mid-August, but historically finished its season early for the World Cup in late September.
The best comparison is the 2021 Tokyo Olympics, when the league went on a break about 19 games into the season, and returned to play 13 over the final month. The No. 6 Sky and No. 5 Mercury became the lowest-seeded teams to reach the Finals.
"I do think that break is good for our league," Fever guard Sophie Cunningham , who played on that Mercury squad, said last month. "I think you're going to see a really competitive playoff game and competitiveness in each series this year, just because you kind of have that extra break for people to rest their bodies a little bit."
Teams had four games amid a tight playoff race to get back to work, and head into the postseason or offseason on a small ramp-up period. It almost feels as though the playoffs have already started, with the rest of the field playing meaningless games to determine how to approach next season.
There is no clear contender in the field. It took until late Tuesday night to clinch the postseason's first seed, when the Valkyries' loss gifted the Lynx the honor of No. 1 overall. The range of possibilities for seedings over the final week were wild to look at, with some teams able to finish as high as 2 and as low as 8.
The games themselves have also been closely contested. At the World Cup break, the league averaged 5.69 lead changes per game, second only to 5.83 in 2010.
The league experienced a historic offensive explosion in 2026, a result of talent, changing styles and rule adjustments. The numbers league-wide are up across the board, including scoring average (87.1 ppg), assists (20.6 apg), pace (83.1), offensive rating (104.9), effective field goal percentage (51.6) and true shooting (56.0).
Six teams are on pace to finish in the top 10 of offensive rating, led by a record-shattering 116.5 by the Indiana Fever . They're averaging a record-setting 97 ppg, over three points more than the 2010 Phoenix Mercury (93.9) and the 2023 Aces (92.8).
Minnesota (112.3) also toyed with breaking the 2019 Mystics' offensive rating record (114.6), but slipped over its final stretch. The Aces (112.7), Dream (112.0), Liberty (111.4) and Wings (110.9) are on their heels.
It's fueled by a flurry from the 3-point line. Four teams rank top five all-time in 3-point makes per game: the Valkyries (10.6, second), Fever (10.4, third), Liberty (10.3, fourth) and Fire (10.2, fifth). The Dream, Aces, Lynx and Liberty finished top 10 in average scoring in league history.
Historic offenses by the 2019 Mystics, 2023 Aces and 2022 Aces went on to win championships. Will that carry over to one of these teams? Will defense indeed win the championship? Is just enough at certain moments the winning amount?
The league's defensive rating is higher than 2025's 105.4. If not for the Valkyries' league-best 99.1 defensive rating, it would have been the first time in league history that not a single team allowed, on average, fewer than 100 points per 100 possessions.
The Dream and Liberty are two franchises heading in opposite directions but carrying the same goal: Get out of the first round.
Atlanta is a franchise on the rise. After a 2025 first-round upset to the injury-plagued Fever, the Dream traded for All-Star Angel Reese as a final piece to get over the hump. Their addition of veteran champion DeWanna Bonner last month gives them additional floor spacing and experience.
They are going all-in for a run at the title after losing in the first round in three consecutive seasons. The last time they made the semifinals was 2018, when they automatically advanced into it as the No. 2 seed in the old format. Their last "series" playoff win came in 2016.
The Liberty are attempting to quell a downslide. In 2023, New York reached its first Finals in two decades, and in 2024, the Liberty won the franchise's first-ever WNBA championship. But a year ago, they floundered amid injuries during the regular season and, as the No. 5 seed, couldn't make it out of the first round of a coast-to-coast three-game series with Phoenix.
They retained their trio of Jonquel Jones , Breanna Stewart and Sabrina Ionescu , though free agent addition Satou Sabally was limited and eventually ruled out for the season. In the offseason, they moved on from Sandy Brondello to first-time head coach Chris DeMarco. This time, a first-round exit could spell a deeper reconstruction.

Minnesota: Would win record fifth WNBA championship and first since 2017. The Lynx won four in seven years with a Hall of Fame core.

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday after a federal judge ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore their press access.
The re-entry came after a chaotic morning, during which the three outlets filed an emergency request for a hearing, accusing the Trump Administration of having “repeatedly violated” the court order and refusing several reporters access to the White House grounds. "This morning, journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in the court document.
Judge Timothy Kelly had given the Trump Administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond to the outlets' filing.
In a court filing of its own, the White House said it "began the process" of reinstating press badges shortly at 7:25 a.m. ET and laid out a timeline of what followed. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Early Thursday, in a District of Columbia court, Judge Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” He ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ​ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning .
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge over the ban and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted : “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
“Either the preliminary injunction will be issued or denied,” says Eugene Volokh, a law professor at UCLA who specializes in the First Amendment. “The temporary restraining order would then lapse, and whichever side loses can then appeal to the D.C. Circuit.”
Instead of an appeal, Trump could file for emergency relief from the D.C. court, similar to how CNN, MS NOW, and Politico did Thursday, according to experts.
But “emergency relief is usually harder to get than a resolution through appeal,” says Volokh.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.
Volokh says that legal precedent in the D.C. Circuit, used in both the ongoing case and that of Acosta, has “already been set” for areas of the White House usually open to the media, including the press briefing room.
“The government can't exclude reporters based on viewpoint, and cannot take away a press pass without due process, without some sort of hearing opportunity to be heard, an explanation of what it is that they supposedly did wrong, what rules they violated,” he says.
In light of this, an appeal from the Trump Administration after a preliminary injunction would likely be rejected in the D.C. Circuit, he argues. However, the President may find a better chance in the Supreme Court.
“Generally speaking, the First Amendment does not secure a right of access to government office buildings,” says Volokh, once again noting the exception of areas usually granted access for press. "The same position could be taken by the Supreme Court, and [it] might say: 'Look, the government can pick and choose whom to allow on its property,'" he says.
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said : “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post —announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips
One is an authoritarian who represses the media and has a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.
Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”
While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.
And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.
That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.
The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X : “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?
“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”
Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.
Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.
Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.
Trump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip ​to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.
The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”
He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.
Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.
But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!
Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will send two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.
Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.
But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”
Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).
None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?
Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.
When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.
Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported : “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.
By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

articles.title_orig: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.title_zh: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

WASHINGTON/NEW YORK/TOKYO -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump have concluded their second formal summit of the year amid continuing tensions over tariffs, rare-earth minerals, artificial intelligence and more.
Four months after Trump traveled to Beijing in May, the two presidents met this time in Washington. The White House welcomed the Chinese leader in elaborate fashion, including a state dinner. Soon after Xi arrived in the Washington, the U.S. said the two sides had agreed to extend their trade truce , which had been due to expire Nov. 10.
But expectations of broader breakthroughs were modest, and the immediate results did little to shift perceptions. Trump and Xi are due to meet again at the APEC forum in Shenzhen in November, and at the G20 Summit in Miami in December.
Nikkei Asia followed Xi's visit live.

The devices are known as optical transceivers. Supporters of the legislation say the devices could be used by Beijing to disrupt access to U.S. AI tools and the cloud, Reuters writes. The restriction would apply to optical transceivers made by China's Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight . "We shouldn't rely on China for technologies that are essential to our national security," one of the lawmakers, Dave McCormick, says in a statement.
1:17 p.m . On his Truth Social platform, Trump bids farewell to Xi. "Much has been, and will be, accomplished," Trump writes. "I look forward to our next meeting!"
1:10 p.m. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, board their plane at Joint Base Andrews, concluding their three-day visit to the United States.
12:15 p.m. Trump and Xi exchange a final handshake after a National Archives tour before Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, head to the airport.
11:20 a.m. Xi attends a tea ceremony with Trump. The Chinese leader says that he will welcome the U.S. president to come to China for the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November and that he expects to meet with Trump again at the Group of 20 meeting in December. Trump says he will go to Shenzhen and that the two will "speak a lot." Xi says the prospects of relationships will get "brighter."
9:45 a.m. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer tells CNBC that details of the latest U.S.-China trade agreements will be released Monday.
Greer says Washington and Beijing reached deals covering a "subset" of non-sensitive goods that could receive more favorable trade terms, without specifying which products are covered or how tariffs might change.
8:50 a.m. Trump says on Truth Social that he had a "very productive meeting" with Xi and that "tremendous things will be happening." He does not provide further details.
7:20 a.m. The U.S. has yet to confirm details of yesterday's closed-door bilateral summit, but footage shows that Vice President JD Vance was among the officials in the room. This marks the potential 2028 presidential candidate's first known formal encounter with the Chinese leadership since taking office.
6:30 a.m. The coast guard of the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, accused China on Friday of obstructing a resupply mission to its troops in the South China Sea, Reuters reports. A spokesperson said dangerous maneuvers by Chinese vessels "put Filipino personnel at risk" and prevented the mission from being completed, although there were no collisions or injuries. This is the latest of numerous confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the disputed waters .
4:30 a.m. At the National Archives, the last scheduled stop of Xi's visit before his departure from Washington, the leaders will have a chance to view some of the most important documents in American history, including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. In addition, Trump has said they will see "artifacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship" between China and the U.S.
Analysts suggested to Reuters that Xi may want to see documents related to the U.S. decision to switch recognition to the People's Republic from Taiwan in 1979.
2:20 a.m. Taipei's Ministry of Foreign Affairs pushes back , after Xi told Trump that China wants the U.S. to uphold the "correct position" of opposing "Taiwan independence" and appeared to link the matter to overall relationship stability.
The Taiwanese ministry says Xi's comments are consistent with a pattern of "distorting facts" and stresses that the Chinese Communist Party "has no right to represent the Taiwanese people." It emphasizes democracy and insists Taiwan will continue to work with the U.S. and other partners to safeguard peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait.
2:00 a.m. As Xi's visit to Washington enters its final hours, economic pressures back home in China loom in the background. A recent high-profile tie-up deal between two major Chinese state-owned carmakers has raised the possibility of broader consolidation across the world's largest car market, analysts say, as Beijing's patience with chronic overcapacity in the industry wears thin.
11:30 p.m. Kolas Yotaka, a former spokesperson for Taiwan's presidential office, writes on X: "If 'one country, two systems' is the relationship China wants with Taiwan, then this new concept of "constructive strategic stability" is the relationship China wants with the U.S.," referring to the formulation for governing Hong Kong and Beijing's framing of its current ties with Washington. "Only difference? Taiwan doesn't accept China's terms. The U.S. just did. That's dangerous for Taiwan."
Yotaka, who is also an author, independent consultant and former legislator, suggests China is trying to box Trump in. It is "using this to demand the U.S. recognize its claim over Taiwan and delay arms sales -- or else it 'threatens' this new 'stability.' That would blow up the status quo."
9:50 p.m. According to the Trump administration, tomorrow's events will kick off when the presidents reconvene at the White House at 10:30 a.m. Trump and first lady Melania will have tea with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan. Later in the morning, they will pay a visit to the National Archives, concluding Xi's state visit.
9:45 p.m. Here's some footage from the summit so far.
8:30 p.m. While dinner is underway, Chinese supporters and anti-China protesters are stationed outside the White House, separated by a few blocks. Groups of Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans and Chinese rights activists waving Tibetan flags chant "Free Hong Kong" and "Stop the Uyghur genocide," while supporters play the Chinese national anthem.
8:15 p.m. Xi begins his remarks by wishing everyone a happy mid-autumn festival, a Chinese occasion celebrating family traditions and reunions.

As China rapidly expands its wind projects near coastal areas, researchers find the turbines can complicate marine vessel detection at sea
Offshore wind farms can reduce the coverage of shore-based radar systems and create areas where targets become harder to detect, according to a new study.
The researchers found that at a range of 5km (3 miles), effective radar coverage fell by 6.9 per cent while blind spots increased by 14.9 per cent.
The research, published online last month in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Radio Engineering, was conducted by Professor Liu Zunnian and his team from Qingdao Technological University and the Yantai Communication Centre of the Beihai Navigation Security Centre under the Ministry of Transport.
The team found that large arrays of wind turbines could produce false “ghost” targets through reflected radar signals, potentially complicating the detection of vessels in coastal waters.

articles.title_zh: Trump declares $1B canceled in ‘pocket rescission’ affront to Congress’ funding power
articles.content_orig:
President using rare power to revoke expenditure with bipartisan approval to aid immigrant services
Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s office of management and budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending”.
Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic president Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by senator Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Collins said in a statement the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions”.
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
“This is theft from the American people, plain and simple,” Patty Murray, the Washington Democratic senator, who is vice-chair of the appropriations committee said in a statement . “These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people – not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families. Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because [Russell] Vought is saying their votes don’t count.”
Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The government accountability office has called the maneuver , known as a “pocket rescission,” illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse”.
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9bn in congressionally approved foreign aid. The US supreme court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a pocket rescission fits part of a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the US government, eroding the power of Congress.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

Presley was signed to IMG Models and appeared in a 2018 Pepsi ad with his mother.

'When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,' she told Vogue .

Xiang Yu’s razing of the Qin capital Xianyang, which left libraries full of vital texts in ruin, was echoed centuries later in Warsaw
Warsaw’s wartime destruction was not merely the consequence of battle, but a deliberate campaign by its Nazi German occupiers to erase much of the city. In August 1944, the Warsaw Uprising – a Polish armed revolt by the city’s underground resistance against German occupation – began with the aim of liberating Warsaw. German forces fought to crush it, subjecting the city to sustained bombardment.
When the uprising was finally suppressed after nine weeks, the surviving population was expelled, with tens of thousands of Poles sent to concentration camps. The emptied city was then systematically destroyed. German demolition units moved through Warsaw, wrecking or blowing up buildings that had survived the fighting. Churches, palaces, schools, theatres, libraries and historic monuments were reduced to rubble.
By January 1945, almost 90 per cent of the city’s buildings had been destroyed. The cultural losses were particularly devastating. Libraries containing centuries of Polish manuscripts, books, maps and other collections were deliberately burned, while countless works of art and historical records vanished. Warsaw was left in ruins, its historic centre a smouldering pile of debris.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects Republicans’ Missouri redistricting push for third time
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects Republicans’ Missouri redistricting push for third time
articles.content_orig:
Court puts end to long-running legal dispute as it rules Republican-friendly map cannot be used in November
The supreme court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by Donald Trump , putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is under way in the midterm elections.
The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.
The supreme court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri supreme court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.
“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. “The district court and court of appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri.”
Republicans had hoped the new House map – which already was used in the August primaries – could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.
A panel of the eighth US circuit court of appeals ruled on Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the US constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order’s effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the supreme court.
The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters – nearly one in four statewide – who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts, though some local election officials had urged voters to wait because of the legal uncertainty.
Republicans currently hold six of Missouri’s eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican governor Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.
The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by longtime Democratic congressman Emanuel Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s fifth congressional district far eastward into rural Republican areas.
The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri’s other congressional districts.
Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state senator Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican congressman Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the eighth circuit’s ruling and the last two appeals to the supreme court.
At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri’s congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their US House districts over the past year.
Missouri’s new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact . In one case, the Missouri supreme court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.
Republican secretary of state Denny Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on 4 August – the day the new districts were used in the primaries – to reject the petition. He asserted referendum petitions aren’t allowed for congressional redistricting.
The Missouri supreme court ruled on 3 September that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The supreme court let that ruling stand on 8 September. But minutes later, US district judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.
The supreme court on 10 September blocked Clark’s order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri supreme court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark’s order.
But that wasn’t the end of the matter. The eighth circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark’s blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That’s what led to the latest decision from the US supreme court.

At the conclusion of Xi's visit, CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer if the leaders achieved anything new on artificial intelligence.
"I wouldn't say anything new," Greer said. Most important thing is having a channel."
Greer said there would be "another meeting on AI in the next month or so" although the agenda has not yet been set.
Though Mr. Trump declined to answer shouted questions from reporters about Taiwan during Xi's visit, U.S. ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is "no change" in the United States' policy toward Taiwan.
" There's no change, no change in the Taiwan policy here," Perdue told CNBC Friday. "He's fully committed to the One China policy. We're committed to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiques, and the six assurances. Nothing has changed there. Of course, China has tried to coerce change in that regard. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there."
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."

articles.title_orig: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
articles.title_zh: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
articles.content_orig:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.
Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.
"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.
Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.
He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".
"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.
A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".
Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached
The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief.
It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.
But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.
However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.
The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.
The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations. US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has requested military support from Trump.
During his speech at the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
On Friday, Araghchi said Iran did not accept "coercion, threats or intimidation" and added that "peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation".

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users in latest example of rogue activity
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users in latest example of rogue activity
articles.content_orig:
Disclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agents
Two ⁠months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.
The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to ⁠say when the images were posted.
Also on Friday, OpenAI confirmed its agents had accessed US government websites, including those of the Security and Exchange Commission and the commerce department, accessing US Census data from the latter. The company was also investigating an attempted breach of the education department’s website, as reported by the New York Times.
The disclosures reveal a ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.
As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated ⁠that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activity and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.
OpenAI said its review would take “months” to complete given the scale of the work, and said it had notified “dozens” of third parties about improper activity.
Most of the leaked images have been ⁠taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.
OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for ​training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.
Before user posts are ‌used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out ‌metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.
But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might ‌leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.
In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or – just on Wednesday – by Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister, at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.
The 21 July announcement that OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by ​their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.
OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On 16 September, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain”.
Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers.
Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.
Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to ⁠include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.
Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that ​went unnoticed by the company for months.
Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives”.
In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement”. Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.
Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday.

Donald Trump pulled out all the stops for his glamorous State Dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping as the two spent much of his visit discussing the toughest issues facing their nations.
The lavish black-tie affair in the historic East Room stands as one of the most star-studded evenings of the administration, offering a glitzy opportunity to smooth over notoriously fierce geopolitical friction with the superpower.

However, the two nations remain divided on the war in Iran and are still grappling to find common ground on trade and how to best navigate the jarring advances of artificial intelligence .
During talks with Xi in Washington ahead of the dinner, the two sides discussed the Iran War, according to state broadcaster China Central Television.
Trump has argued to little effect that Beijing , which is far more dependent on Gulf oil than the US, has plenty of incentive to use its sway with Tehran to help force an end to the conflict.
But the President's war of choice has unnerved China, with the government condemning American and Israeli military action and Xi previously expressing concerns that the conflict signaled a return to what he called the 'law of the jungle.'
The US administration has warned the country, which is Tehran's biggest trading partner, not to aid Iran's military effort.
